source.title: Graph Theory. Favorite Conjectures And Open Problems - 1 [PDF]

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a regular graph in which no two vertices belong to the same number of triangles?

evidence.quote: Erd˝os, Székely, and Trotter (Personal communication, 2014) showed that there are, in fact, infinitely many K3 -irregular graphs, that is, no two vertices belong to the same number of triangles. Whether there exist regular K3 -irregular graphs is unknown. Problem 4.5. Does there exist a regular K3 -irregular graph?

accepted.question_text: For a given positive integer n, which subsets S of the positive integers can occur as exactly the path lengths k for which some connected graph G of order n is k-path irregular, meaning that whenever two vertices u and v are connected by a path of length k, the degrees of u and v are different?

evidence.quote: For a positive integer k, a connected graph G is k-path irregular (see [4]) if deg u ¤ deg v for every two vertices u and v connected by a path of length k in G. ... Problem 5.6. For a given positive integer n, which sets S of positive integers have the property that there exists a connected graph G of order n that is k-path irregular if and only if k 2 S?

accepted.question_text: Given a connected graph G = (V, E), can its vertex set be partitioned into two sets S and V − S such that both parts are nearly perfect, where a set S is nearly perfect when every vertex in V − S is adjacent to at most one vertex in S?

evidence.quote: A set S  of vertices in a graph G D (V, E) is nearly perfect if every vertex in V  - S is adjacent to at most one vertex in S.
NEARLY PERFECT BIPARTITION INSTANCE: Connected graph G D (V; E). QUESTION: Can the vertices of G be partitioned into two sets V D {S; V - S} such that both S and V - S are nearly perfect sets?

accepted.question_text: Given a connected graph G, does G contain a disconnecting matching, that is, a matching whose removal disconnects G?

evidence.quote: Thus, we seek a disconnecting matching, that is, a matching M, the removal of the edges in which it disconnects G. This in turn gives rise to the following, equivalent, decision problem: DISCONNECTING MATCHING INSTANCE: Connected graph G D (V; E) QUESTION: Does G contain a disconnecting matching?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a polynomial-time algorithm that decides whether a triangle-free graph embedded on a fixed surface is three-colorable?

evidence.quote: Problem 4. Does there exist a polynomial time algorithm that decides if a trianglefree graph embedded on a fixed surface is three-colorable?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a surface S that admits infinitely many four-critical graphs of girth five embedded on S?

evidence.quote: Problem 5. Does there exist a surface S and an infinite number of four-critical graphs of girth five that embed on S?

accepted.question_text: If S_g denotes the largest chromatic number needed among orientable genus-g surfaces formed by gluing convex polygons together so that adjacent faces are not coplanar, is S_g bounded above by a constant independent of g?

evidence.quote: An Sg -polytope is an orientable surface of genus g made by gluing convex polygons together so that adjacent faces are not coplanar. The chromatic number of such a surface is the fewest number of colors needed to color the regions so that adjacent regions are given different colors.
For a fixed g, let us refer to the largest chromatic number needed to color an Sg -polytope as the chromatic number of Sg and denote it (Sg). ... Problem 6. Is (Sg) = O(1)?

accepted.question_text: If S_1 is the largest chromatic number needed to color an orientable genus-1 polytope of the kind defined in the source, is S_1 at most 4?

evidence.quote: David Barnett [4] showed that (S1) ≤ 6. And Thomassen replaced this six with five [52]. This leads me to ask: Problem 7. Is (S1) ≤ 4?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a permutation A = (a1, a2, a3, ...) of the positive integers such that the sequence of absolute consecutive differences D = (d1, d2, d3, ...), where di = |a_{i+1} - a_i|, is also a permutation of the positive integers?

evidence.quote: Let N D {1, 2, 3, : : : } denote the set of positive integers. A permutation of N is a sequence A D {ak | k ∈ N} D (a1, a2, a3, : : : ) in which every element of N appears exactly once. The difference sequence of A is D D (d1, d2, d3, : : : ) where di D |ai+1 - ai|. One of the questions asked by Roger Entringer is the following. Does there exist a permutation A of N such that the difference sequence D is also a permutation of N?

accepted.question_text: Suppose that for 1 ≤ i ≤ n there are n cliques K_n(i) on vertex sets V_i such that any two distinct vertex sets intersect in at most one vertex. Must the union of these n cliques have chromatic number n?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2.1 (EFL: graphical). If, for 1 ≤ i ≤ n, the n-cliques Kn(i) on vertex sets Vi satisfy |Vi ∩ Vj| ≤ 1 for i ≠ j, then the union G = ⋃_{i=1}^n Kn(i) has χ(G) = n.
